title: Data coverage over time
shows: Number of loads per day in each file.
finding: Training covers 01 Jan – 31 Oct 2025; validation covers 01 Nov – 31 Dec 2025. No overlap; volumes are steady (~160/day train, ~200/day validation).
decision: Validation must be time-based (train on the past, score the future). A random split would leak same-day market conditions into training.

title: Missing values by column
shows: Share of missing values per column in each file.
finding: weight: 300 train / 165 validation missing; market_index: 374 / 249. Every other column is complete, including the target.
decision: No rows dropped for missing features. market_index -> that day's median (it is a market-wide signal); weight -> left as NaN for LightGBM (native handling) plus a missing flag, and equipment median for the linear stage.

title: Target distribution
shows: Histogram of posted_rate on the dollar scale and on the log scale.
finding: Range $57 – $25,533, median $2,031. Strongly right-skewed with a long tail of extreme values.
decision: Model log(rate): errors become relative (a $50 miss matters more on a $300 load than a $3,000 one), multiplicative effects (equipment premium, market index) become additive, and the tail has less leverage.

title: Rate vs distance (log–log)
shows: Each point is one load (flagged anomalous labels removed), coloured by equipment.
finding: A straight line on log–log axes means a power law: rate ∝ distance^0.87. Distance alone explains 99% of the variance in log(rate).
decision: log(distance) is the primary feature. A power below 1 means rate per mile falls with distance.

title: Rate per mile by distance and equipment
shows: Median $/mile per distance band (line) with the 10th–90th percentile band (shaded).
finding: Median $/mile: Dry Van 2.05, Flatbed 2.22, Reefer 2.31. The ordering holds at every distance, so equipment acts as a roughly constant % premium.
decision: Equipment enters as a multiplicative premium (dummy variables on log scale).

title: Equipment mix and price level
shows: Left: share of each equipment type per file. Right: $/mile distribution (outlier labels removed).
finding: Mix is ~57% Dry Van, 25% Reefer, 18% Flatbed in both files; no category appears only in validation.

title: Weight: sign errors and a cap
shows: Left: raw weight including negatives. Right: weight after taking the absolute value.
finding: 292 train and 145 validation weights are negative, with magnitudes (median 31,822 lb) matching normal loads ⇒ sign errors, not a separate population. 2.5% of loads sit exactly at 47,500 lb (a cap).
decision: Take abs(weight) and keep a 'was negative' flag. Keep the capped values (a legal-limit cap is plausible and the model sees it as 'heaviest').

title: Effect of weight on price
shows: Mean residual of a distance-only fit, by weight band (shown as % difference).
finding: Smooth, monotonic, roughly logarithmic relationship. Weight is a real but modest driver.
decision: Use log(weight) in the linear stage and raw weight in the tree stage.

title: Train vs validation: covariate shift
shows: Density of each numeric feature in train_test.csv and validation.csv.
finding: distance, weight and quote_signal match closely. market_index is the exception: validation sits in a narrow low band (0.72–1.10) vs 0.68–1.47 in training — but fully inside the training range.
decision: Validation inputs are covered by training data, so no feature has to be extrapolated except time itself.

title: Market index over time
shows: Left: daily median market_index (grey) and 7-day mean. Right: average by weekday relative to the period mean.
finding: Two components: (1) a slow regime — rises Jan–May, plateaus, falls Aug–Sep, flat Oct–Dec; (2) a very regular 7-day cycle peaking Wed–Thu (±12%) that is identical in train and validation. Within a single day loads differ by only ~0.025.
decision: Treat market_index as a market-wide daily signal: impute by daily median and also give the model each load's deviation from it.

title: quote_signal
shows: Left: distribution. Right: mean residual of a distance-only fit by quote_signal vigintile.
finding: Correlation with $/mile is only 0.10. The effect is U-shaped: almost flat (about −2% to +1%) for the middle 80% of loads, rising to +4–8% only in the thin tails (quote_signal < 1.6 or > 2.5). A linear term cannot capture a U-shape.
decision: Keep it: its linear coefficient is near zero, but the tree stage can learn the U-shape.

title: Correlations between features and target
shows: Pearson correlation between numeric features, log(rate) and rate per mile.
finding: log_distance dominates log_rate (r = 0.99).  Among the rest, market_index, weight and equipment correlate with $/mile; features are not strongly correlated with each other, so multicollinearity is not a concern for the linear stage.

title: City locations and unseen cities
shows: Each city's coordinates as given in the data. Stars = cities that never appear in training.
finding: 72 cities. Unseen in training: Allentown, Charlotte, Chicago, Jackson, Knoxville, Laredo, Norfolk, San Diego. 1,447 validation loads (12%) touch at least one of them.
decision: City name cannot be a model feature (no training rows for 8 of them). Describe lanes by coordinates, distance and circuity instead, which exist for every city.

title: Are the coordinates real?
shows: Arrows from each city's approximate real location to where the dataset puts it (18 well-known cities).
finding: Displacements are large (median 144 miles; Phoenix is moved ~395 miles). So coordinates are synthetic/perturbed, not real geography. However each city has exactly one coordinate pair, and the distance column is consistent with them (median distance ÷ great-circle = 1.18, a typical road-circuity factor).
decision: Treat coordinates as dataset-internal location signals, not real geography. Do not join external data (e.g. real regional rate indices) on them. This corrects the earlier report wording.

title: Lane coverage
shows: Left: how many training loads each pickup→delivery lane has. Right: validation loads on lanes with/without training history.
finding: Median lane has only 10 loads, and 12% of validation loads are on lanes never seen in training.
decision: Lane-level target encoding would be noisy (few loads per lane) and unavailable for 12% of validation. Use smooth geographic features that generalise between lanes.

title: Circuity (road vs straight-line distance)
shows: Ratio of the distance column to the straight-line distance between the coordinates.
finding: Median 1.18; rises above 1.4 only for short lanes (<150 miles straight-line). No impossible values (ratio < 1).
decision: The distance column is trustworthy. Circuity is added as a feature for the tree stage.

title: Calendar patterns in price
shows: Mean residual of a distance-only fit by weekday and by month.
finding: Weekday pattern mirrors the market_index weekly cycle (Wed–Thu highest). Month pattern rises through spring, peaks in June, dips in Aug–Sep and recovers in Oct.
decision: Both are largely explained by market_index; the remainder is studied in the date-effect analysis (validation section).

title: Anomalous price labels
shows: Left: ratio of each actual rate to a robust (Huber) log-linear expectation. Right: number of loads flagged as the threshold changes.
finding: Normal loads all fall within ±19% of expectation. Then there is an empty gap, and 677 loads (1.4%) sit at 0.2–0.5× or 2–5×. Every threshold from 1.20× to 2.19× flags exactly these rows. They are spread evenly across months, equipment types and distances, and their features look normal.
decision: Treat them as anomalous labels (likely data-entry or unit errors, but not proven) and exclude them from training; the threshold choice does not matter. Still report metrics with them included.

title: History of the December chart lane
shows: Every training load on Lexington → Fort Wayne (the fixed lane in the December chart).
finding: 32 loads, $758–$974, mixed equipment and weights (dry van only: 21 loads, $758–$934).
decision: Sanity reference for the December chart: predictions around $820–$860 for a 32,000 lb dry van sit inside this historical range.

title: Validation design
shows: Three expanding-window folds plus the final fit. Dates are inclusive.
finding: Each fold reproduces the real task: everything before a cut-off is training data, the next two calendar months are scored. The final model is trained on all of Jan 1 – Oct 31 and predicts Nov 1 – Dec 31, the same 2-month horizon.
decision: Same folds, rows and metrics for every model compared; outlier detection is re-fitted inside each fold on training months only.
